background.definition: Personality disorders are psychiatric disorders characterized by chronic patterns of inner experience and behavior that are inflexible and present across a broad range of situations. They have a marked impact on patients’ interpersonal relationships, and social and occupational functioning, and can lead to problematic interactions in the medical setting.

list.listitem: The lifetime prevalence of personality disorders in the general population is between 10% and 13%.
The prevalence of personality disorders in primary care outpatient settings is between 20% and 30%.
In male prisoners, the prevalence of antisocial personality disorder is 60%.
A systematic review of antisocial personality disorder concluded that it is more common in patients with bipolar disorder, and is associated with a higher risk of criminal behavior and addiction.
Genetic predisposition: major character traits are thought to be inherited.
Environmental factors: other traits result from a combination of genetics and environment.
Unknown.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Pregnancy: viral and bacteria infection, alcohol or drug use, nutritional deprivation

list.listitem: An unblinded randomized controlled trial that began in 1991 identified children with conduct problems, and compared a comprehensive treatment intervention with usual care. In adulthood, the result was a lower likelihood of psychiatric problems, crime conviction, and high risk sexual behavior. B
Suspect personality disorder in difficult patients who have long-standing biopsychosocial issues. C

When you suspect a personality disorder, conduct a comprehensive biopsychosocial interview and consider referring for psychological testing with the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI). B
Interview relatives and friends to establish enduring patterns of behavior. C
Perform the Mini-Mental State Examination or Montreal Cognitive Assessment to screen patients for dementia if clinically suspected. B

A personality disorder must meet the following diagnostic criteria: (1) An enduring pattern of inner experience and behavior that deviates markedly from the expectations of the individual’s culture. This pattern is manifested by two (or more) of the following areas: cognition, affectivity, interpersonal functioning, and impulse control; (2) The enduring pattern is inflexible and pervasive across a broad range of personal and social situations; (3) The enduring pattern leads to clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning; (4) The pattern is stable and of long duration, and its onset can be traced back at least to adolescence or early adulthood; (5) The enduring pattern is not better accounted for as a manifestation or consequence of another mental disorder; (6)The enduring pattern is not due to the direct physiological effects of a substance or general medical condition.

Personality disorders fall into three clusters (below). See for a comprehensive summary of typical features and management options. Cluster A: paranoid, schizoid, and schizotypal; Cluster B: antisocial, borderline, histrionic, and narcissistic Cluster C: avoidant, dependent, and obsessive-compulsive
The typical presentation of different personality disorders is summarized in .
In older patients, consider dementia in the differential diagnosis and use a validated screening instrument such as the Mini-Mental State Examination.
Psychological testing (eg, the MMPI-II) is recommended.

Consider the following studies if clinically indicated: urine screen to rule out substance abuse; neuropsychological tests to ascertain the presence of a learning disorder or dementia; and thyroid-stimulating hormone and venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) tests. Brain imaging (including CTs and MRIs) is not considered a first-line diagnostic strategy, but can be used to ascertain the presence of a structural neurological abnormality when one is clinically suspected.
When personality disorder is suspected, conduct a comprehensive interview of the patient, relatives, and friends to establish enduring patterns of behavior.

Conduct a physical examination and screen older patients for dementia using the Mini-Mental State Examination. Laboratory and imaging studies should only be considered when organic brain disease like a frontal lobe tumor is clinically suspected.
Conduct a risk assessment to rule out harm to self, and harm to others, and consider consultation with a psychiatrist.
Use multidisciplinary treatment teams, and treat personality disorder as a chronic condition. B

Consider individual psychotherapy (eg, cognitive behavioral therapy [CBT], dialectical behavioral therapy [DBT], psychoanalytic therapy), group therapy, or family therapy for patients with any personality disorder. B
Psychotherapy effectively reduces symptom severity for patients with borderline personality disorder, but no specific psychotherapy is superior. A
Psychotropic medications are used as adjunctive therapy; choose drug therapy according to target symptoms (). B

Psychotropic medications are viewed as an adjunctive treatment in the management of personality disorders that can be helpful for some symptoms in some patients. Choose drug therapy according to target symptoms: Cluster A and Cluster C have straightforward and limited target symptoms and medication options; Cluster B has multiple groupings, or subclusters, of target symptoms and potentially more complicated medication regimens. See for medication options.
Large studies are lacking, but small controlled studies suggest that patients with schizotypal, borderline, and avoidant personality disorders may respond to medications.

A randomized trial of 95 patients with borderline personality disorder (BPD) found that quetiapine 150 mg significantly reduced symptom severity compared to placebo (response rate 82% vs 48%, p = 0.007, NNT = 2). A higher dose was not more effective but had more side effects. However, a Cochrane review found very low-certainty evidence that pharmacological therapies for BPD are no better than placebo for the primary outcomes of symptom severity, self-harm, suicide-related outcomes, and psychosocial functioning.

A Cochrane review of 11 RCTs found insufficient evidence for the efficacy of pharmacological interventions to treat antisocial personality disorder, citing signficant methodological flaws in the included studies.

Work in multidisciplinary teams for all three clusters of personality disorders. Psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, marriage and family therapists, case managers, nurses, and medical doctors should work together to establish diagnosis, implement, and carry out treatment, and provide ongoing care.

Systemic observation and treatment enhance the care of the patient and reduce the potential burnout of the primary care doctor working with the patient with a personality disorder; the interpersonal behavior of the patient may elicit strong emotional reactions in the physician.
A systematic review of mostly very low quality studies (cross-sectional, case series, qualitative, and observational) suggested benefit to music therapy.

Outpatient individual psychotherapy is recommended for the management of symptoms in all three clusters of personality disorders. A systematic review of 54 trials found a large effect size (g= 0.78) for a range of psychological therapies delivered in the outpatient setting.

Group psychotherapy is also recommended specifically for Cluster B and Cluster C because it uses therapeutic confrontation and increases a patient’s awareness and insight into the damaging effects of dysfunctional behavioral patterns.

Family therapy is indicated for all types of personality disorders to establish a baseline of the enduring personality disorder pattern, to facilitate communication among family members regarding the inherent stressors related to the functioning of the family member with a personality disorder, and to monitor progress and behavior changes.

A Cochrane review involving 75 RCTs enrolling 4507 patients with borderline personality disorder (BPD) found psychotherapy to be effective, compared to usual treatment, in improving all primary outcomes, including BPD symptom severity, self-harm, suicide-related outcomes, and psychosocial functioning. But of all primary outcomes, only BPD symptom severity achieved a clinically meaningful improvement based on pa redefined cutoff. aThe mority of thychological interventions involved dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) and mentalization-based treatment (MBT). The authors did not find any difference between the various psychotherapies. Other systematic reviews found similar findings.
A systematic review identified 10 randomized trials of psychological therapies for BPD in adolescents. Most found no benefit, and the overall quality of evidence was described as very low.
Schema therapy, which focuses on identifying unhealthy ways of thinking and overlaps with cognitive behavioral therapy, appears effective for BPD.
A Cochrane review identified only poor quality completed trials of interventions for acute crisis in persons with BPD. Better quality trials are underway.

A Cochrane review of 19 RCTs evaluating psychological interventions for adults with antisocial personality disorder found very limited evidence for their effectiveness. Only 3 trials showed DBT, contingency management with usual care, and schema therapy to be more effective than control. However, no psychological intervention improved antisocial behavior.

A randomized trial of 642 patients with personality disorder randomized them to treatment as usual or a "whole of service stepped care approach" that attempted to divert them toward psychological therapy clinics rather than hospital. It was successful, reducing hospital bed days from 13.5 to 4.3 days per admission. It was also cost-saving.

A Cochrane review of community mental health teams (CMHTs) for patients with severe mental illnesses and personality disorders found CMHT to be noninferior to nonteam-based care for important outcomes. More importantly, CMHT appears superior in reducing suicide deaths and hospital admissions, and in promoting treatment acceptance by patients, compared to nonteam-based care.

Democratic therapeutic communities were found to be effective at 2 years in a small RCT, primarily for reducing self- and other directed aggression and improving satisfaction with care. These communities are a form of group therapy that focus on inquiry and forming relationships between members.

A trial randomized 246 adults with depression and comorbid personality disorder to either 25 weekly or 50 biweekly sessions of either short-term psychoanalytic supportive psychotherapy (SPSP) or schema therapy in a 2x2 factorial trial. The more intensive 50 session arms had higher rates of remission of depression (74% vs 58%, p = .025, NNT = 7) as well as higher rates of remission from personality disorder (74% vs 56%, p = .01, NNT = 6).
For patients with borderline personality disorder, though, a secondary analysis of a Cochrane review found little effect of pharmacotherapy on depressive or anxiety symptoms.
Psychiatric consultation should be considered for patients with an unclear diagnosis, for complex treatment regimens, or for refractory symptoms.

Personality disorders are chronic conditions; the goal is to manage the symptoms, not cure them. Because personality disorders by their very nature are enduring patterns of behavior, the prognosis for these patients depends on how well their symptoms are managed. B
If the symptoms are well managed, 50% of patients with a personality disorder can live independently. B
A systematic review of 18 studies found that patients with comorbid personality disorder responded equally well to pharmacotherapy for mood disorders. B

feature.caption: Personality Disorders: Manifestations and Management Strategies.
feature.feature_body:
Personality Disorder Prominent Features of the Disorder Problematic Behaviors in Medical Setting Management Strategies
Cluster A: Odd or Eccentric
Paranoid Distrust, suspicion; begins in early childhood; heightened sense of fear and vulnerability Fear physician, may harm, argumentative, conflicted Adopt a professional stance, provide clear expectations, be empathic to fears, avoid direct challenge to paranoid ideation
Schizoid Social detachment and emotional restriction; anxiety because of forced contact with others Delay seeking care, appear unappreciated Adopt a professional stance, provide clear explanations, avoid overinvolvement in personal and social issues
Schizotypal Odd beliefs/interpretations and eccentricities, socially isolative; social and interpersonal deficits; anxiety because of forced contact with others Delay seeking care, odd beliefs, odd behavior Adopt a professional stance, provide clear explanations, tolerate odd beliefs and behaviors, avoid overinvolvement in personal and social issues
Cluster B: Dramatic, Emotional, or Erratic
Antisocial Disregards and violates rights of others; lack of remorse for wrongdoing; lack of empathy; sense of entitlement masks fear Anger, impulsive behavior, deceit, manipulative behavior Carefully investigate concerns and motives, communicate in a clear manner, set clear limits
Borderline Instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affect; marked impulsivity; terrifying fantasies about illness Fear of rejection and abandonment, self-destructive acts, idealization and devaluation of physician Avoid excessive familiarity; schedule regular visits; provide clear, nontechnical explanations; tolerate angry outbursts, but set limits; maintain awareness of personal feelings; consult psychiatrist
Histrionic Excessive attention-seeking behavior and emotionality; threatened sense of attractiveness and self-esteem Overly dramatic, attention-seeking behavior, inability to focus on facts and details, somatization Avoid excessive familiarity, show professional concern for feelings, emphasize objective issues
Narcissistic Grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy; anxiety caused by doubts of personal adequacy Demanding, attitude of entitlement, denial of illness, alternating praise and devaluation of physician Validate concerns, give attentive and factual responses to questions, channel patient’s skills into dealing with illness
Cluster C: Anxious or Fearful
Avoidant Social inhibition due to fears of rejection or humiliation; feelings of inadequacy and low self-esteem; hypersensitivity to criticism Withholds information, avoids questioning or disagreeing with physician Provide reassurance, validate concerns, encourage reporting of symptoms and concerns
Dependent Excessive need to be taken care of, submissive and clinging behavior; fear of separation; fear of abandonment/helplessness Urgent demands for attention, prolongation of illness behavior to obtain attention and care Provide reassurance, schedule regular check-ups, set realistic limits on availability, enlist others to support patient, avoid rejection of patient
Obsessive-Compulsive Preoccupation with orderliness, perfection, control; mental and interpersonal control; fear of losing control of bodily functions and emotions Fear of relinquishing control, excessive questioning and attention to details, anger about disruption of routines Complete thorough history and examinations, provide thorough explanations, do not overemphasize uncertainty, encourage patient participation in treatment
Adapted from Personality disorders. In: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th ed. Washington, DC: American Psychiatric Association; 2000: 689.
